strengths: ReVisiT offers a simple, relevant contribution to multimodal generation: reuse cached vision-token representations, select a reference through constrained Jensen–Shannon divergence, and combine its distribution with the decoder output. It requires neither retraining nor an additional model forward pass per generated token.

Evaluation covers three hallucination benchmarks, two dense LVLMs, and an additional DeepSeekVL2 experiment. Reported object-hallucination improvements are reasonably consistent: LLaVA CHAIR-I decreases from 14.66 to 13.43, Qwen from 8.51 to 7.56, and DeepSeekVL2 from 7.04 to 2.10.

Reporting object recall and AMBER coverage alongside hallucination metrics helps expose informativeness tradeoffs. The vocabulary-constraint ablation also candidly demonstrates a severe generation failure rather than interpreting its low hallucination rate as success.

The latency study specifies hardware, warmup, repeated measurements, and variability. Its reported decoding latency is close to greedy decoding and substantially below the evaluated contrastive baselines.
weaknesses: Reproducibility remains incomplete in consequential ways. Appendix A.2 gives an alpha search range and default but omits the actual task-specific settings and the validation procedure used to select thresholds and layers. DeepSeekVL2 settings are also insufficiently specified. Because Table 4 shows sensitivity to these choices, the distinction between held-out tuning and benchmark-specific selection matters, especially when competing methods use default settings.

The central efficiency claim needs fuller accounting. Algorithm 1 caches a matrix of size |J| × |v| × |V|, potentially substantial for Qwen's multiple layers, large vocabulary, and high-resolution inputs. Peak memory, projection/precomputation time, and end-to-end latency are not reported, and it is unclear whether the per-token timings include cache construction. These omissions prevent verification of the claimed memory efficiency and broadly negligible overhead.

Several improvements are small and lack uncertainty estimates. Qwen CHAIR-S improves from 32.2 to 31.6 on only 500 images, and average POPE accuracy improves from 84.49 to 84.77. Qwen recall decreases on CHAIR, while LLaVA AMBER Hal slightly worsens. Paired confidence intervals and output-length statistics would help establish reliable gains and clarify coverage tradeoffs; the results do not support uniformly superior performance.

The experiments do not isolate the proposed selection mechanism. Comparisons against random vision-token selection, average vision-token distributions, alternative selection criteria, and mismatched-image references would test whether minimum-JSD selection contributes specifically grounded information rather than generic distributional reweighting. Selected qualitative examples alone provide limited support for identifying the chosen token as the most visually relevant reference.

The implementation description contains a mathematical inconsistency: Equation 8 normalizes a product of probabilities, whereas Algorithm 1 applies softmax directly to that product. These preserve the same greedy argmax but define different sampling distributions. The paper also raises robustness across decoding methods without actually evaluating non-greedy generation.

The claimed fine-grained grounding evidence exceeds the evaluation presented. AMBER's reported generative metrics concern object mentions and do not establish improved attribute or relation reasoning. Appendix A.1 also incorrectly describes higher Cog as desirable, contrary to Table 3. Overall, the empirical contribution is promising, but unresolved reproducibility and efficiency-accounting concerns prevent a clear Findings recommendation.

strengths: ReVisiT addresses a relevant problem in multimodal language generation with a simple, training-free approach: cache vocabulary projections of vision-token hidden states, select a reference through constrained Jensen–Shannon divergence, and combine its distribution with the decoder output.

The evaluation includes generative and discriminative benchmarks, two primary model families, and an additional DeepSeekVL2 experiment. Comparisons with DoLa, VCD, M3ID, and SID provide useful context.

The results support a promising empirical contribution. LLaVA POPE accuracy improves from 79.47 to 81.80, while DeepSeekVL2 CHAIR-I decreases from 7.04 to 2.10 with a comparatively small recall reduction. Improvements are therefore not uniformly attributable to suppressing object mentions.

The paper provides equations, pseudocode, evaluation prompts, a CHAIR sampling seed, detailed POPE results, and a vocabulary-constraint ablation. Runtime measurements specify hardware, warmup, repeated measurements, and variability.
weaknesses: Reproducibility and tuning fairness remain insufficiently established. Appendix A.2 gives an alpha search range and default, but not the exact task/model settings used throughout the main experiments or the held-out procedure for selecting them. This matters because Table 4 shows that changing alpha can reverse the improvement over greedy decoding. ReVisiT receives empirical configuration selection while baselines use their original defaults, leaving the comparison sensitive to unequal tuning.

The central efficiency claim needs fuller accounting. Algorithm 1 caches a matrix of size |J| × |v| × |V|, potentially substantial when using multiple Qwen layers and high-resolution images. The paper reports per-token latency but does not clearly establish whether the initial vocabulary projections are included, and provides neither peak-memory measurements nor time-to-first-token and end-to-end results. The reported decoding latency supports a narrower claim than broadly negligible computational overhead or memory efficiency.

Several gains are small and lack uncertainty estimates. On 500 CHAIR images, Qwen CHAIR-S changes from 32.2 to 31.6—three fewer hallucinated captions—while recall decreases from 71.79 to 70.83. Its average POPE accuracy improves by only 0.28 points, and its F1 remains below SID. Paired confidence intervals or significance tests would help distinguish reliable improvements from sample variation.

The evidence for the proposed selection mechanism is limited. Table 4 tests vocabulary restriction, layer pools, and alpha, but does not compare minimum-JSD selection against random selection, averaged vision-token references, or other inexpensive selection rules. Qualitative examples show that projected tokens can contain useful information; they do not establish that agreement with the current prediction reliably identifies the most visually relevant token rather than reinforcing existing model biases.

Some claims exceed the evaluation. AMBER is described as validating fine-grained attribute and relation grounding, but the reported generative metrics measure object mentions and coverage rather than directly demonstrating those capabilities. Improvements are also not uniform: LLaVA AMBER Hal increases from 32.7 to 33.0. All quantitative experiments use greedy decoding, so robustness across decoding methods is not established.

The algorithm description contains a consequential inconsistency: Equation 8 normalizes a product of probabilities, whereas Algorithm 1 applies softmax to that product. These preserve the same greedy argmax but define different sampling distributions. This should be corrected without implying that it invalidates the reported greedy results. Overall, the empirical promise makes Findings plausible, but unresolved tuning, reproducibility, and efficiency-accounting concerns prevent a clear positive recommendation.

strengths: ReVisiT addresses an important multimodal generation problem with a simple, training-free approach: reuse projected vision-token representations, select a reference through constrained Jensen–Shannon divergence, and refine the next-token distribution. Avoiding additional decoder passes is a useful practical contribution.

The experiments provide meaningful evidence of reduced object hallucination across generative and discriminative benchmarks. LLaVA’s average POPE accuracy improves from 79.47 to 81.80, while the additional DeepSeekVL2 experiment reduces CHAIR-I from 7.04 to 2.10 with a comparatively modest recall decrease.

Reporting object recall and coverage alongside hallucination metrics helps assess whether improvements merely reflect less informative outputs. The vocabulary-constraint ablation also transparently exposes severe generation degeneration when this component is removed.

The paper provides mathematical definitions, pseudocode, benchmark prompts, a CHAIR sampling seed, detailed POPE results, and repeated latency measurements. These are useful foundations for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Task-specific hyperparameter selection is insufficiently documented. Appendix A.2 provides an alpha search range and default, but not the exact settings for every model–benchmark combination or the held-out data and criterion used for selection. DeepSeekVL2 settings are also incomplete. Because Table 4 demonstrates substantial sensitivity to alpha, these omissions prevent a clear assessment of reproducibility and tuning fairness against baselines using default settings.

The central efficiency claim needs fuller accounting. Algorithm 1 caches a matrix of size |J| × |v| × |V|, which can be substantial for Qwen’s multiple layers, large vocabulary, and variable image resolution. The timing protocol does not clearly establish whether initial projection and cache construction are included. Peak memory, time to first token, and end-to-end latency across image resolutions and output lengths are needed to support the claimed negligible overhead and memory efficiency.

Several improvements are small or mixed, without uncertainty estimates. On Qwen, CHAIR-S improves from 32.2 to 31.6 on 500 images—three fewer hallucinatory captions—while recall declines from 71.79 to 70.83. Average POPE accuracy improves by 0.28 points, and F1 remains below SID. LLaVA’s AMBER Hal slightly worsens. Paired confidence intervals would help distinguish reliable improvements from sample-specific variation.

The ablations establish the importance of vocabulary restriction but do not isolate the proposed reference-selection mechanism. Comparisons with random vision-token selection, pooled vision representations, alternative selection rules, and mismatched-image references would clarify whether minimum-JSD selection actually identifies useful visual evidence rather than primarily reinforcing existing model preferences.

There are methodological and reporting inconsistencies. Algorithm 1 applies softmax to a product of probabilities, whereas Equation 8 requires division by their sum; these produce different sampling distributions, although their greedy argmax agrees. The introduction describes top-K restriction while Equation 5 uses relative probability thresholding. The claimed robustness across decoding methods is unsupported because the quantitative experiments use greedy decoding.

The broader grounding claims exceed the demonstrated scope. The reported AMBER generative metrics concern object mentions and do not establish improvements in attribute or relation hallucinations; selected qualitative examples likewise cannot establish general reasoning improvements. Overall, the empirical contribution is promising, but unresolved configuration and efficiency-accounting issues make this borderline for Findings rather than a clear acceptance.

strengths: ReVisiT addresses a relevant problem in multimodal language generation with a simple, training-free intervention: select a vision-token projection using constrained Jensen–Shannon divergence and combine it with the next-token distribution. The method requires no additional model forward pass during decoding.

The evaluation covers five benchmarks, six decoding baselines, and additional CHAIR experiments across seven model configurations. Promising results include reducing Qwen2.5-VL-7B CHAIRS from 35.2 to 29.8 while increasing object F1 from 79.85 to 81.16, and improving LLaVA HallusionBench qAcc from 11.55 to 20.22.

The appendix provides useful metric definitions, a CHAIR sampling seed, pseudocode, detailed results, and component ablations. Reporting object F1 alongside hallucination rates helps expose degenerate methods that avoid hallucinations by producing little useful content.
weaknesses: Reported results contain unresolved inconsistencies with the stated evaluation protocols. Appendix A.2 defines MMMU accuracy as binary correctness averaged over 857 items, implying increments of approximately 0.117 percentage points; Table 5's Qwen improvement from 51.11 to 51.18 cannot arise under that definition. HallusionBench's overall accuracy also cannot consistently be reconstructed from its Easy and Hard accuracies using fixed split sizes: the LLaVA greedy row implies an Easy proportion of approximately 7.7%, whereas the ReVisiT row implies 31.8%. The evaluated subsets, aggregation procedures, and tables need reconciliation before the benchmark evidence is dependable.

Hyperparameter selection and reproducibility are insufficiently documented. The paper specifies a search range for alpha but does not give the actual model-by-benchmark settings or identify a separate tuning split. Layer selections for the additional model configurations are also missing. VQAv2's evaluated split and sample count are unspecified. Consequently, one cannot reproduce the reported comparisons or assess whether task-specific tuning on evaluation data contributed to the gains.

The interpretation experiments do not adequately isolate image-specific semantics. Restricting predictions from approximately 151,000 tokens to 176 object synonyms naturally increases object recall, and matching any object present anywhere in the image does not establish local token grounding. Frequency-matched, shuffled-image, or mismatched-reference controls would distinguish visual information from vocabulary restriction and object priors. The reported Wilson intervals and token-level significance tests also ignore dependence among tokens from the same image or caption.

The efficiency evidence establishes low reported per-token latency but does not substantiate the broader claims of negligible inference cost and memory efficiency. Algorithm 1 caches a matrix of size |J| times |v| times |V| and requires projecting every selected vision-token hidden state across the vocabulary. The timing protocol does not clearly state whether this initialization is included, and there are no peak-memory, time-to-first-token, or end-to-end measurements. These costs matter particularly for short responses, high-resolution images, and larger layer pools.

The strength and consistency of the improvements are overstated. Qwen MMMU gains only 0.07 percentage points, Qwen HallusionBench overall accuracy gains 0.68 points, and SID substantially outperforms ReVisiT on Qwen POPE F1. LLaVA-13B CHAIRS worsens from 48.0 to 52.6. Paired uncertainty estimates for benchmark differences and a held-out tuning protocol are needed to establish which gains are reliable.

Algorithm 1 applies softmax to a product of probabilities, whereas Equation 6 requires dividing that product by its sum. These operations preserve the greedy argmax, so this discrepancy need not invalidate the deterministic experiments, but they define different probability distributions and sampling behavior. The implementation and mathematical description should agree. Overall, the promising contribution needs important evaluation and reproducibility revisions before a sound Findings recommendation is warranted.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant multimodal NLP problem with a simple, training-free decoding method. Constrained vision-token projection, minimum-JSD selection, and multiplicative refinement form a concrete approach that avoids additional model forward passes.

The evaluation covers five benchmarks, several decoding baselines, and additional CHAIR experiments across seven models. Reported improvements include Qwen2.5-VL-7B CHAIR sentence-level hallucination decreasing from 35.2 to 29.8 and F1 increasing from 79.85 to 81.16.

Reporting caption object F1 alongside hallucination rates is valuable: the ablations explicitly expose configurations that obtain low hallucination scores by producing uninformative outputs. The appendix also provides useful metric definitions, qualitative examples, and a fixed CHAIR sampling seed.
weaknesses: Evaluation numbers need reconciliation with the stated protocols. In Table 2, overall HallusionBench accuracy should be a fixed weighted average of Easy and Hard accuracy under Appendix A.2. However, the LLaVA greedy values imply approximately 7.7% Easy examples, while the Qwen greedy values imply approximately 61.5%, despite using the same split. Table 5 also reports MMMU accuracies incompatible with the stated binary accuracy over 857 items: 35.13% and 51.18% cannot result from an integer number of correct answers at that sample size. These discrepancies could reflect reporting or aggregation errors, but they currently prevent confident interpretation of central results.

Important reproduction and model-selection details are missing. Appendix A.4 gives an alpha search range and default, but not the actual model-by-benchmark settings or a held-out selection protocol. VQAv2's evaluated split and sample count are unspecified, and configurations for the additional models are incomplete. Since baselines use original default hyperparameters while ReVisiT receives task-specific adaptation, the comparison also needs a clearer account of tuning fairness.

The mechanistic evidence does not isolate image-specific semantics sufficiently. Restricting prediction from 151,665 vocabulary entries to 176 object synonyms naturally raises object recall; the magnitude alone does not establish visual grounding. Image-shuffled references, frequency-based controls, and comparisons with equally sized alternative subsets would distinguish image information from vocabulary restriction and object priors. Likewise, finding any annotated object among alternative predictions does not establish that it is a valid replacement at that particular hallucinated position.

The efficiency claim is incompletely supported. Algorithm 1 caches a matrix with |J| × |v| × |V| entries, making memory and initial projection costs potentially substantial, especially for multiple layers and high-resolution inputs. Table 12 reports per-token latency without clearly separating or accounting for this precomputation. Peak memory, time to first token, and end-to-end latency for short and long outputs are needed to support 'minimal computational overhead' and scalability.

The main performance comparisons lack uncertainty estimates, despite several small margins: Qwen MMMU improves by 0.07 percentage points and HallusionBench overall accuracy exceeds SID by 0.17 points. The statistical analyses supplied for the motivation treat correlated tokens or vision patches from the same image as independent observations; image-level resampling would provide more defensible uncertainty. Generality should also be qualified: LLaVA-13B sentence-level CHAIR worsens from 48.0 to 52.6, and SID remains stronger on Qwen POPE accuracy and F1.

Algorithm 1 applies softmax to a product of probabilities, whereas Equation 6 requires dividing that product by its sum. These yield different distributions, although their argmax agrees under the reported greedy decoding. This should be corrected and the implemented operation specified. Overall, the promising method warrants revision, but the evaluation inconsistencies and reproducibility gaps prevent a sound Findings recommendation at present.

strengths: ReVisiT addresses a relevant NLP problem with a simple, training-free decoding intervention: select a vision-token projection using constrained Jensen–Shannon divergence and combine it with the output distribution. The method requires neither retraining nor an additional model forward pass during each decoding step.

The empirical coverage is substantial: five benchmarks, six decoding baselines, and additional CHAIR experiments covering seven models across three architecture families. Including caption-level F1 alongside CHAIR hallucination rates helps detect improvements obtained merely by suppressing object mentions.

Several reported gains are meaningful. LLaVA-1.5-7B HallusionBench question-pair accuracy rises from 11.55 to 20.22, while Qwen2.5-VL-7B CHAIR sentence-level hallucination decreases from 35.2 to 29.8 with improved F1.

The vocabulary and selection ablations support the practical importance of combining constrained projection with minimum-divergence selection. The appendix supplies useful metric definitions, qualitative examples, a CHAIR sampling seed, and timing measurements.
weaknesses: Evaluation reporting contains an important unresolved inconsistency. Appendix A.2 defines MMMU accuracy as binary correctness averaged over 857 examples, implying increments of approximately 0.1167 percentage points. Several Table 5 values, including 35.13 and 51.18, cannot result from that denominator after rounding. The actual evaluation population, aggregation procedure, and underlying correct counts need clarification before the claimed improvements can be trusted.

Reproducibility and tuning independence are insufficiently established. Appendix A.4 supplies a search range for alpha but not the selected values for every model–benchmark combination or a held-out selection protocol. Layer settings for the additional models are also unspecified, and the VQAv2 evaluation split and sample count are missing. Comparing task-adapted settings against baseline defaults further requires a clear account of the tuning budget.

The interpretability evidence does not adequately isolate image-specific semantics. Restricting prediction from 151,665 tokens to 176 object synonyms mechanically improves object recall; random-ranking, frequency-prior, and mismatched-image controls are needed to establish the additional contribution of visual representations. Moreover, matching any object anywhere in the image does not establish spatial alignment of an individual vision token. The Wilcoxon tests and Wilson intervals also treat correlated tokens from the same images as independent; image-level resampling would better quantify uncertainty.

The efficiency claim is incomplete. Algorithm 1 caches a matrix with |J| × |v| × |V| entries, introducing potentially substantial memory and initial projection costs. The reported per-token timings do not clearly establish whether cache construction is included. End-to-end latency, time to first token, peak memory, and scaling with image resolution are needed to support the broader claim of negligible computational overhead.

The breadth of the positive conclusions exceeds the evidence. Qwen's MMMU improvement is only 0.07 points, and its HallusionBench overall advantage over SID is 0.17 points, without paired uncertainty estimates. SID substantially exceeds ReVisiT on Qwen POPE F1, and LLaVA-1.5-13B sentence-level hallucination worsens from 48.0 to 52.6. Consistent CHAIR F1 improvements therefore do not establish uniformly reduced hallucination.

Algorithm 1 applies softmax to a product of probabilities, whereas Equation 6 specifies normalization by their sum. These preserve the same greedy argmax, so this discrepancy alone does not invalidate the reported deterministic experiments, but they define different probability distributions. Overall, the approach is promising, but the evaluation inconsistency and missing experimental specifications require important, plausibly next-cycle revisions before a sound and reproducible Findings recommendation.
